newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Traders see vast potential in Russian bank shares.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Traders see vast potential in Russian bank shares.

text.p: The illiquid market for Russian bank shares will soon follow the rapidly developing market for industrials as banks needing cash make new share issues and foreign investors get to know them better.
"The second half of 1997 and 1998 will be the year of bank shares," said Dmitry Lobanov, chief trader at IK Alfa-Capital.
In the next one or two years bank shares will make up at least 20 percent of the total Russian market compared with 2.8 percent now, he said.
Current bank share market capitalisation is about $1.5 billion with $1.0 billion in Russia's biggest bank Sberegatelny Bank Rossiiskoi Federatsii (Sberbank) shares, he said.
Total market capitalisation is about $54 billion.
Sberbank was the only bank stock to take part in a January rally, rising to $141 on March 4 from about $50 at the end of 1996, said Vadim Koblyakov, a Unitrust trader.
The market has huge potential as banks in need of cash will make more issues, Lobanov said.
The Central Bank has tightened its grip on commercial banks by issuing new requirements for banks to be introduced gradually over the next two years.
They must raise minimum capital of five million Ecu by July 1, 1998, from two million on April 1, 1996.

Sergei Gerasimov, a Russian Brokerage House trader, said it will also become easier to trade bank shares as banks will have to switch to a computerised system of share registration from the present paper-based system.
Sberbank has already computerised the registration of a recent issue and is registering others on computer.
American Depositary Receipts issues, made by AB Inkombank recently and planned by MAKB Vozrozhdeniye and Bank Menatep, will also help the market develop, Lobanov said.
"At least we have been receiving questions about what these banks are from foreign clients for the last two months," he said.
Bank Vozrozhdeniye, with branches in almost every region, was in narrow but steady demand, while Promstroibank Rossii had the most growth potential, Lobanov said.
TRADING IN SBERBANK REAPS HIGH PROFITS
Traders said they favour state-run Sberbank as they count on government support in a sector going through hard times. One said he expected it to rise to $200 by the end of March.
Sberbank, the former monopoly Soviet savings bank which
still dominates retail banking, is the market's favourite because it can boast 4.33 trillion roubles (about $7.73 billion) in 1995 profits and about 400,000 branches, they said.

Sberbank is effectively the only banking share traded on Russia's electronic Russian Trading System. It is quoted on its new lower tier RTS-2 PAUFOR12. Bank St Petersburg is listed on the main RTS, but is rarely traded.
"In fact, the market now only consists of Sberbank," Lobanov said.
An investment in Sberbank eight months ago would have yielded an annual return of 2,700 percent in hard currency without dividends, he said.
TRADING BANK SHARES NOT EASY
Investors in Russian bank shares may encounter difficulties they do not face in other sectors.
The Russian Central Bank has set up a time-consuming and difficult procedure for selling bank shares to foreigners.

"For a foreigner, speculative possibilities here are about the same as in Gazprom," Koblyakov said, referring to Russia's natural gas monopoly which requires permission from the company's board to sell its shares.
Banks own their own registrars, which is usually illegal, and the registrars are often hostile to investors, a trader said.
Sberbank does not encourage trading of its shares. It sells them to employees and considers a sale a breach of loyalty to the company, Gerasimov said.
But bank shares will attract interest because they are so undervalued, Lobanov added.
Trinfiko trader Ilya Galtsov said the fact that Sberbank's 1995 profit was higher than its total market capitalisation testified to its potential.
"The prospective for growth is immense."
